lead: A uniform linear array (ULA) is N identical elements on a straight line with equal spacing d, equal current amplitude and a constant phase step α from one element to the next. Adding elements narrows the beam and raises directivity without making any single element larger. With α = 0 the beam is broadside, at right angles to the line; with α = −βd it is end-fire, along the line. Sector panels on mobile towers are broadside arrays; a long end-fire array suits a mast or a boom that points at the target.
prereq: You need: the two-element array factor and pattern multiplication from two-element arrays, and beamwidth and directivity from the antenna fundamentals topic.

sections.h3: The array factor of N elements

blocks.text: Number the elements 0 to N − 1 along the z axis. Element n has current I e<sup>jnα</sup>, and its wave reaches a far point in direction θ (measured from the axis) ahead by nβd cosθ. Every neighbour pair therefore differs by the same ψ = βd cosθ + α, and the array factor is a geometric series:

blocks.where: The sum of N unit phasors, each turned ψ further than the last.
AF<sub>n</sub> is the array factor normalized to 1 at ψ = 0; N is the number of elements; ψ = βd cosθ + α in radians.

blocks.text: The main lobe is at ψ = 0. Nulls are at Nψ/2 = ±mπ, that is ψ = ±2πm/N with m = 1, 2, … but not a multiple of N. Between nulls lie sidelobes; for N = 4 the first sidelobe is 0.272 of the peak (−11.3 dB), and for large N it tends to −13.3 dB. When ψ reaches ±2π inside the visible range (βd + α down to −βd + α), the phasors line up again and a second full-size beam, a grating lobe, appears.

Broadside: α = 0, so ψ = βd cosθ and ψ = 0 at θ = 90°. The beam is a disc around the array axis. The first nulls satisfy cosθ = ±λ/(Nd). The visible range is ±βd, so a grating lobe (ψ = ±2π) appears at the ends of the axis once d ≥ λ.

Ordinary end-fire: α = −βd, so ψ = βd(cosθ − 1), which is 0 at θ = 0°. The beam points along +z, toward the lagging end; α = +βd turns it to θ = 180°. The visible range is now 0 down to −2βd, so a grating lobe at the back (ψ = −2π at θ = 180°) appears once d ≥ λ/2. An end-fire array therefore needs d < λ/2, and λ/4 is the usual choice.

Hansen-Woodyard end-fire: some syllabi add α = −(βd + π/N). The extra phase makes the beam narrower and raises directivity about 1.8 times above ordinary end-fire, at the cost of higher sidelobes and a tight tolerance on the phase.

For a long array (Nd ≫ λ) the standard estimates are below. They come from setting the array factor to 0 (first nulls) or to 0.707 (half power) and solving for θ; the end-fire beam is wider because cosθ changes slowly near θ = 0°.

Both beamwidths depend on the array length Nd in wavelengths, not on N alone. The end-fire array has twice the directivity of a broadside array of the same length because its single beam is a pencil along the axis instead of a disc all around it.

examples.question: A 4-element broadside array has spacing d = λ/2 and equal in-phase currents. Find (a) the main-beam direction, (b) the first nulls and the first-null beamwidth, (c) the half-power beamwidth, and (d) the level of the first sidelobe.
steps: βd = π and α = 0, so ψ = π cosθ. The visible range is −π to π.
(a) ψ = 0 gives cosθ = 0, so the beam is at θ = 90°.
(b) First nulls: ψ = ±2π/4 = ±π/2, so cosθ = ±0.5 and θ = 60° and 120°. FNBW = 120° − 60° = 60°. The formula agrees: 2 sin⁻¹(λ/(4 × 0.5λ)) = 2 sin⁻¹(0.5) = 60°.
Second nulls: ψ = ±π gives cosθ = ±1, θ = 0° and 180°.

(c) Half power: sin(2ψ)/(4 sin(ψ/2)) = 0.707 is solved numerically at ψ = ±0.715 rad. Then cosθ = ±0.715/π = ±0.228, so θ = 76.8° and 103.2° and HPBW = 26.3°. The long-array estimate 50.8/(Nd/λ) = 50.8/2 = 25.4° is close.
(d) The sidelobe between the first and second null peaks at θ = 42.9° (and 137.1°) with |AF<sub>n</sub>| = 0.272, that is 20 log 0.272 = −11.3 dB.
examples.answer: Beam at 90°, first nulls at 60° and 120° (FNBW 60°), HPBW 26.3°, first sidelobe −11.3 dB at 42.9° and 137.1°.

examples.question: Ten isotropic elements are spaced λ/4 apart (Nd = 2.5λ). Compare a broadside and an ordinary end-fire design: give α, FNBW, HPBW and directivity for each.
steps: Broadside HPBW ≈ 50.8/2.5 = 20.3° (the exact pattern gives 20.5°). D ≈ 2 × 2.5 = 5, that is 7.0 dBi (exact 5.17).
End-fire: α = −βd = −π/2 = −90° per element, increasing lag toward +z.
End-fire D ≈ 4 × 2.5 = 10, that is 10.0 dBi. Grating-lobe check: d = λ/4 < λ/2, so the back end is clear.
examples.answer: Broadside: α = 0, FNBW 47.2°, HPBW about 20.3°, D ≈ 5 (7 dBi). End-fire: α = −90°, FNBW 106.3°, HPBW about 69.3°, D ≈ 10 (10 dBi). The end-fire beam is wider in angle but, being a single pencil instead of a disc, has twice the directivity.

traps: Using the broadside spacing rule for an end-fire array. Broadside is free of grating lobes up to d < λ; end-fire already has a full back lobe at d = λ/2.
Leaving α out of ψ. A zero of cosθ is the main beam only when α = 0.
Counting the m = N null. Nψ/2 = ±Nπ is ψ = ±2π, a grating lobe, not a null.
Quoting the broadside beamwidth formula for end-fire. End-fire beamwidths use cos⁻¹(1 − …) and are much wider for the same length.
Thinking more elements always means a wider band of nulls. More elements give more nulls, each closer to the beam, and a narrower main lobe.

quiz.q: Write the normalized array factor of an N-element uniform linear array and define ψ.
quiz.a: |AF<sub>n</sub>| = |sin(Nψ/2)/(N sin(ψ/2))|, with ψ = βd cosθ + α, β = 2π/λ, d the spacing, θ the angle from the axis and α the progressive phase.

quiz.q: State the phase conditions for broadside and for ordinary end-fire.
quiz.a: Broadside: α = 0 (beam at θ = 90°). End-fire: α = −βd for a beam at θ = 0°, or α = +βd for θ = 180°.

quiz.q: Why does an end-fire array get a grating lobe at a smaller spacing than a broadside array?
quiz.a: With α = −βd the visible ψ range is 0 to −2βd, twice as long on one side as the broadside range ±βd; it reaches −2π at d = λ/2 instead of at d = λ.

quiz.q: A 6-element broadside array has d = λ/2. Find the first nulls and FNBW.
quiz.a: ψ = π cosθ; nulls at ψ = ±π/3, so cosθ = ±1/3: θ = 70.5° and 109.5°. FNBW = 38.9°.

quiz.q: Find α for an ordinary end-fire beam at θ = 0° when d = λ/4 and f = 3 GHz. What is d in centimetres?
quiz.a: λ = 10 cm, so d = 2.5 cm. βd = π/2, so α = −π/2 rad = −90° per element.

quiz.q: A 4-element end-fire array has d = λ/4 and α = −90°. Find its nulls.
quiz.a: ψ = (π/2)(cosθ − 1). Nulls at ψ = −π/2 and −π: cosθ = 0 and −1, so θ = 90° and 180°. The beam fills 0° to 90°; HPBW = 2 × 57.0° = 114°.

quiz.q: A broadside array is built with d = λ. What happens, and how would you fix it without changing the array length?
quiz.a: At θ = 0° and 180°, ψ = ±2π, so grating lobes as large as the main beam appear along the axis. Halve d to λ/2 and double N; the length Nd and the main beam stay the same while the grating lobes vanish.

quiz.q: How does changing α from −βd to +βd move an end-fire beam?
quiz.a: With α = +βd, ψ = βd(cosθ + 1), which is zero at θ = 180°. The beam flips to the other end of the axis, toward the element that now lags.

beyond: Not for the exam. A planar array is two linear arrays multiplied together, one along each edge, and that is how 5G and radar panels with dozens of elements are analysed. Adaptive arrays change their weights while running, with algorithms such as LMS or MVDR, to put nulls on interferers. Grating lobes have an imaging cousin, spatial aliasing, studied in array signal processing. Search for planar array factor, adaptive beamforming and spatial aliasing.
